newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - Far East takes honours in stock index poll.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Far East takes honours in stock index poll.

text.p: The Far East should hold the greatest allure for international equities investors both this year and next, with Hong Kong looking set to be the best performing major bourse over the period despite the uncertainty over its return to Chinese rule, a Reuters survey showed on Wednesday.
Analysts said they expected sluggish performances from the U.S. and most European stock markets.
Reuters surveyed 108 analysts in 14 countries between March 10 and 13 to gauge their expectations for the world's 15 largest stock exchange in terms of market capitalisation.
Enthusiasm for U.S. stocks has been dampened by expectations of a rise in interest rates and the possibility of firms failing to live up to earnings forecasts, the survey found.

Ten analysts who gave predictions for the Dow Jones Industrials put the index at an average of around 7,100 by the end of this year, while the average prediction from nine analysts for the Nasdaq index averaged around 1,300.

Although sluggish, this forecast is slightly less bearish than a similar Reuters survey three months ago, when the average outlook was for a six percent fall in both the Dow and Nasdaq indices by the end of the year.
Analysts predicted cautious progress in the Dow for 1998, up to around 7,500 by the end of the year, although Nasdaq was seen barely changed.
"The broader market is not looking good...Interest rates are going up, probably to 7.5 percent, and the market won't take that well," said Harry Laubscher, analyst at Tucker Anthony in New York.

The story was similar in London, with an average end-97 FTSE forecast little changed from current levels. Analysts said the likelihood, according to opinion polls, that the opposition Labour party would win the May 1 election was sending jitters through the market.

"Interest rates are going to go up sharply (after the election). There may be a lull in domestic demand at the moment, but the second half of this year will be much more active and the government will have to react with higher interest rates," said Richard Jeffrey, group economist at Charterhouse.
But Tokyo shone as the favourite choice among the world's top three indices. The Nikkei 225 was forecast to pick up towards the end of 1997 and then consolidate in 1998.

In all, Nikkei watchers in the poll made an average prediction of nearly a 15 percent rise from current levels to more than 21,000 by the end of next year. They said the Japanese market would be driven by government plans to promote deregulation and administrative reforms.

"The likely economic slowdown in the April to June period should be a one-off event. The economy should rebound afterwards, led by higher private spending," said Tadahire Kamogawa, general manager at Yamaichi Securities in Tokyo.

But the star of the East was Hong Kong's Hang Seng index, which all of the Hong Kong analysts said should this year coast through its all-time closing high of 13,868.24, which it hit on January 20 this year.
A mean of six forecasts collected from Hong Kong-based equities analysts showed that the index would be just under 15,000 points by the end of the year, a 14 percent increase from current levels.
This is forecast to be dwarfed by further rises in 1998, and an average of five forecasts showed the Hang Seng soaring by 35 percent from current levels to around 17,800 by the end of next year.

Main engines for growth after the British colony's return to Chinese rule on July 1 are expected to be continued economic growth in China, a reasonably strong U.S. economy and core countries in Europe emerging from their economic slowdown.

"China is going to further relax macroeconomic controls, we will see more Chinese funds flowing into Hong Kong - like the property sector and the equity market as well - so the index may overshoot a bit," said Ben Kwong, director of research at Dharmala Securities.
Taiwan's TAIEX bourse index would also benefit from the "greater China" effect, the poll found.
In Europe, the quest to attain the targets set for economic and monetary union (EMU) during 1997 hung like a spectre over equities markets.
Six analysts in the Reuters survey who made forecasts for Germany's DAX-30 index gave an average prediction of a slight drop from current levels by the end of the year.

"European monetary union will not turn out to be a long-term burden. All this talk depresses stock prices. But the economic situation is steadily improving, and this...should make profit expectations improve," said Erhard Schmitt, of Hessische Landesbank in Frankfurt.

The survey showed that Italys BCI index may be hindered in its anticipated upward rise if the country fails to meet the joining requirements for EMU. At the moment Italy is forecast by most analysts to fall short of the debt and budget deficit criteria for EMU entry.
Spanish stocks were projected to enjoy a fillip from the measures being taken by Madrid to ensure EMU membership, the poll found.

"Due to tension over European monetary union, we will see moments of volatility, but we think the market's upside potential is there on the back of the Bank of Spain's capacity to cut interest rates. We'll also be helped by an expected recovery in Germany in the second half," said an equities analyst at Inverban in Madrid.
Many of the analysts said that 1998 forecasts were nigh impossible to maintain owing to market volatility.
"Such projections ... are etched in sand, not in granite," said Alfred Goldman, technical analyst with A.G. Edwards in the U.S city of St Louis.
